Appendix A Cue Search

A.1  Method

  • •

    Propose openings. Beam search extends prefixes one token at a time, retaining 20 openings (beam width) to a maximum of two tokens (depth). Openings are ranked by their probability averaged across the 30 problems.

  • •

    Sample responses. For each prefix, we sample 16 responses to each of 30 MATH training problems, with a 16,384-token budget (Tab. 1).

  • •

    Measure agreement. We normalize final answers with the grader and count their frequencies, assigning missing answers to one category. We compute Shannon entropy in bits for each problem. More agreement among answers gives lower entropy.

  • •

    Select a cue. We discard prefixes whose missing-answer rate across all responses is more than 10 percentage points above the no-cue rate. We choose the remaining prefix with the lowest mean entropy over the 30 problems. No prefix is discarded in these runs.

Reference answers are used only for evaluation.

For Olmo-3-7B under RL-Zero, the 20 prefixes cover approximately 86% of opening probability mass, counting overlapping prefixes once and using the rounded values in Tab. 1. Beam search can miss effective openings that have low probability. Low answer entropy does not imply high accuracy.

A.2  Controls

A.2.1  Larger Search

We expand the search to the 50 most probable first tokens and the ten most probable successors of each. This gives 500 two-token openings. We compare these openings with no cue on Olmo-3-7B under RL-Zero, with 4 rollouts per MATH-500 problem and a 31,744-token budget. The best opening scores 0.784; the selected cue scores 0.773 (Fig. 11). Every higher-scoring opening is a variant of  AyAlright or consists of formatting tokens.

A.2.2  Random Openings

We test five uniformly sampled token pairs and five uniformly sampled tokens after the paragraph break (Tab. 3). The paragraph break alone scores 0.766. Following it with a random token gives 0.333–0.471 across the five draws, below the reasoning cue. All ten random openings produce longer responses and reach the token budget more often than no cue.

A.2.3  Longer Openings

We extend the selected cue by adding the most probable next token one at a time (Fig. 12). Extending the cue adds little accuracy and reduces it once the opening becomes problem-specific.

A.3  Comparing with Prompt Optimization

We compare token cues with openings optimized by GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026), which uses an external LLM and graded execution traces to propose revisions. It receives answer labels and correctness feedback, unlike our search.

Setup.

We adapt GEPA to optimize text prefilled at the start of the response (the assistant prefill). In its Appendix C meta-prompt, we replace write a new instruction with write the first few tokens of the assistant’s response, with no length constraint. We use GPT-4.1-mini for reflection, three-problem minibatches, and 300 MATH training problems split into 260 for feedback and 40 for validation. We run this on Olmo-3-7B-Base under the RL-Zero prompt and Qwen3-14B-Base under the boxed prompt, and retain the best prefill by validation performance within 5,000 rollouts. We evaluate on MATH-500, AMC 23, and AIME 2024 using the paper’s shared decoding settings.

Results.

GEPA finds explicit reasoning instructions of 9 tokens for Olmo and 64 for Qwen (Fig. 13). Both improve MATH-500 accuracy, but the short token cues score higher on all three benchmarks in these runs (Tab. 4).

Appendix B Evaluation Protocol

B.1  Sampling and Metrics

Generation.

We use the sampling parameters in Tab. 5 unless stated otherwise. Generation stops at the end-of-text token, at a new Problem: block, or at the token budget.

Grading.

Under RL-Zero, we extract the last Answer: line, stripping surrounding dollar signs. If no such line is found, or if the prompt is boxed or Minerva, we take the last brace-balanced \boxed{...} expression or, if absent, the text after the last “Final answer” marker. Math-Verify (Kydlíček, 2025) checks equivalence with the reference; extraction, parsing or verification failures count as incorrect. For HumanEval, we extract code from fenced blocks or the raw response, remove surrounding prose and prepend the function stub for body-only completions. Correctness requires passing all unit tests.

Metrics.

We report pass@1 as the fraction of correct responses. Its standard deviation is computed across rollout indices on the full benchmark, measuring sampling variation rather than variation across training runs.

Pass@16 estimates the probability that at least one of 16 sampled responses is correct. We use the unbiased estimator of Chen et al. (2021) averaged over problems, with its standard deviation over 1,000 bootstrap resamples of the problems.

Token budget.

The token budget is the maximum generated response length. Cap rate is the fraction of responses that reach it.

Coverage.

In the full benchmark tables, we report a cell only when every problem has all 32 responses generated with the stated token budget.

Response excerpts.

[...] marks omitted text. Lengths and grades refer to full responses. For math excerpts, green, red and gray indicate correct, incorrect and unextracted answers.

B.2  Prompts

We use two zero-shot prompts and one few-shot prompt. All three are plain text with no chat template, and the problem statement replaces {problem}. The boxed prompt uses the Qwen2.5-Math instruction (Yang et al., 2024) in a Problem: / Solution: layout. The RL-Zero prompt is the one Ai2 used to train Olmo-3-7B-RL-Zero-Math (Olmo et al., 2025, Figure 37). We place each token cue at the start of the response and let the model generate the continuation.

⬇
Problem: {problem}
Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.
Solution:
⬇
Solve the following math problem step by step.
The last line of your response should be the answer to the problem in form Answer: $Answer (without quotes) where $Answer is the answer to the problem.
{problem}
Remember to put your answer on its own line after "Answer:"
Minerva 4-Shot.

We use the Minerva 4-shot prompt (Lewkowycz et al., 2022) from the Olmo 3 base-model math evaluations in OLMES (Gu et al., 2025). We prefix each test problem with four fixed worked examples, each labeled Problem: and Solution: and ending with a Final Answer line. The test prompt ends at Solution:. For cued Olmo, we then prefill  Ay\n\n  AyOkay  Ay, . Grading follows the boxed-prompt rules. Our stop rules permit multiple paragraphs, whereas OLMES stops at the first blank line. Below is the first of the four examples; the others use the same format.

⬇
Problem:
Find the domain of the expression $\frac{\sqrt{x-2}}{\sqrt{5-x}}$.
Solution: The expressions inside each square root must be non-negative. Therefore, $x-2 \ge 0$, so $x\ge2$, and $5 - x \ge 0$, so $x \le 5$. Also, the denominator cannot be equal to zero, so $5-x>0$, which gives $x<5$. Therefore, the domain of the expression is $\boxed{[2,5)}$.
Final Answer: The final answer is $[2,5)$. I hope it is correct.
[three more worked examples in the same layout]
Problem:
{problem}
Solution:

B.3  Benchmarks

  • •

    MATH-500. The 500-problem test subset of MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024).

  • •

    GSM8K. 1,319 problems (Cobbe et al., 2021).

  • •

    AMC 23. A 40-problem subset of AMC 12 2023 (AI-MO, 2024b).

  • •

    AIME 2024 and AIME 2025. 30 problems each (AI-MO, 2024a).

  • •

    OlympiadBench. A 300-problem text-only math subset (He et al., 2024).

  • •

    HumanEval. 164 problems (Chen et al., 2021).

Appendix C Reasoning Results

C.1  Benchmark Results

Tabs. 6 and 7 report pass@1 and pass@16 for base and RL-trained models, without a cue and with the opening shown in each block heading. Base-model cues are selected by the search in App. A, with the SmolLM3 boxed-prompt exception described below.

SmolLM3-3B-Base.

We evaluate SmolLM3-3B-Base (Bakouch et al., 2025), whose released weights include a decay stage with reasoning traces (Tab. 6). Under RL-Zero, the search selects  Ay.\n\n  AyThe . Under the boxed prompt, it selects no opening, so we transfer the RL-Zero cue using the boxed format: a space, a paragraph break and  AyThe . This transferred cue improves MATH-500 accuracy under the boxed prompt. The search does not propose  AyOkay , despite its use at the start of the model’s training traces. Placing it after the paragraph break gives 0.47 on MATH-500, compared with 0.51 for the selected cue.

C.2  Figure 1 Responses

Fig. 1 quotes two responses of Olmo-3-7B-Base to one MATH-500 problem, one with  Ay.\n  AyAnswer prefilled and one with  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay , both cut to fit the panel. We show one response excerpt per cue below. All use the RL-Zero prompt, 4 rollouts per problem and a 31,744-token budget. One of the four no-cue responses is correct, none of the four  AyAnswer responses is, and all four  AyOkay responses are.

Response excerpts across different token cues

 

C.3  Base and RL Responses

We compare Olmo-3-7B-Base with and without  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay and its RL-Zero counterpart on a second MATH-500 problem. All use the RL-Zero prompt and a 31,744-token budget. We show all four no-cue base-model responses, which are incorrect, and excerpts from the first cued and RL responses. All four cued responses are correct. Across the 16 RL-Zero rollouts, 9 are correct and 6 reach the token budget.

Base model, no cue

 

C.4  Prompts and Post-Trained Models

Tab. 8 tests cues under a few-shot prompt and in post-trained models. Under Minerva (Lewkowycz et al., 2022), we place the cue after four fixed worked examples and use the boxed-prompt grading rules. For post-trained Olmo, the cue begins the assistant turn. For Qwen3, it follows an empty think block with thinking off, or the opening think tag with thinking on. We also test the Olmo-3-32B RL model under both zero-shot prompts.

Few-shot prompts.

Under Minerva, cues improve the four Olmo and Qwen3 base models by 16–43 percentage points. SmolLM3 shows essentially no change, from 0.380 to 0.382 with the same problems, rollouts and seed, despite improving from 0.193 to 0.506 under RL-Zero.

Post-trained Olmo.

The cue adds 1.6 percentage points to Olmo Instruct and lowers Olmo Think accuracy by 0.1 percentage point.

Post-trained Qwen3.

With thinking off, the cues raise accuracy by 7 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and 6 on Qwen3-14B, while roughly doubling response length. With thinking on, accuracy changes by less than 0.1 percentage point. The base models’ RL-Zero math cues behave differently. These cues,  Ay.\n  AyTo for Qwen3-4B and  Ay.\n\n  AyTo for Qwen3-14B, give no gain with thinking off. With thinking on, they lower accuracy by 10 and 7 percentage points and shorten responses to about a third of their original length.

Olmo-3-32B RL.

The Olmo-3-32B RL model gains nothing under its training prompt but 38 percentage points under the other zero-shot prompt.

C.5  Other Base Models

We test Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B to assess how cue gains vary across model families (Tab. 9).

Llama-3.1-8B.

Under RL-Zero, 94% of Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) rollouts have no extractable answer. None of the tested openings raises accuracy appreciably above zero; the lowest-entropy candidate is the end-of-text token. With Minerva’s worked examples, no-cue accuracy reaches 0.18. Each tested cue—the paragraph break,  Ay␣To , and  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay —reduces this accuracy. The  AyOkay cue also produces longer responses.

Qwen2.5-Math-7B.

Qwen2.5-Math-7B (Yang et al., 2024), which underwent continued pretraining on mathematical text, already writes solutions without a cue. Under RL-Zero, it scores 0.63 with 8% missing answers. The selected  Ay␣To and the paragraph break alone add only 2–3 percentage points.  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay lowers accuracy by 3 percentage points under RL-Zero and 12.3 under Minerva.

C.6  Code

To test whether cues selected on math transfer to code, we evaluate them on HumanEval under both prompts (Tab. 10).

Under RL-Zero, the math cues improve accuracy over no cue on Olmo-3-7B, Olmo-3-32B, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B by 18, 5, 7 and 4 percentage points, respectively. SmolLM3’s selected  AyThe adds 5 percentage points but scores below the paragraph break alone (0.255). In contrast,  AyOkay , which opens its training traces but is missed by the search, raises accuracy from 0.172 to 0.458. Under the boxed prompt, the Olmo cues add 21 and 16 percentage points, while the Qwen cues lower accuracy.

C.7  Cue Variants

The Olmo cue combines a paragraph break with  AyOkay . Either part recovers most of its accuracy gain on Olmo-3-7B under RL-Zero (Tab. 11). The period and blank line alone score 0.766, close to the full cue’s 0.769 and above the no-cue score of 0.415. Without a paragraph break,  Ay␣Okay scores 0.749. Replacing the blank line before  AyOkay with a single newline gives a smaller gain.

The paragraph break has a different effect on refusal (Sec. H.2), so this finding is specific to the math comparison. The rows in Tab. 11 come from the cue-search evaluations; for  Ay␣Okay , we use the first four of its 32 rollouts.

C.8  Paragraph Breaks in Uncued Responses

Responses.

We analyze the 2,000 uncued responses used in Tab. 11: Olmo-3-7B on 500 MATH-500 problems under RL-Zero, with 4 rollouts per problem and a 31,744-token budget. Most responses complete the prompt’s final sentence with a period, followed by a blank line or a single newline. A paragraph break begins 50% of correct responses (415 of 831), compared with 14% of incorrect responses (165 of 1,169; Tab. 12). On the 340 problems with both opening types, responses beginning with a paragraph break are correct 47 percentage points more often than the other responses. This comparison holds the problem fixed but remains observational.

Following tokens.

After a paragraph break, 95% of responses continue with  AyOkay . After a single newline, the most common continuations are  AyAnswer (29%, pass@1 0.14) and  AyProblem (24%, pass@1 0.01). Overall, 28% of responses begin with  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay ; none begins with  Ay␣Okay .

Token probabilities.

On 100 MATH training problems,  Ay␣Okay ranks 542nd on average directly after the prompt, with mean probability 1.3×10−51.3\times 10^{-5}. The paragraph break ranks second (0.24). After it,  AyOkay ranks first on every problem (0.56). Thus, the paragraph-break form follows likely next-token choices, while bare  Ay␣Okay is unlikely despite being effective when forced (Sec. C.7).

Appendix D Reinforcement Learning

We compare standard and cue-forced RL, then analyze changes in opening probabilities and weights. A separate weight edit tests whether increasing cue probability directly can recover the accuracy gain.

D.1  Training Objective and Setup

We train with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) and binary correctness rewards on MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021). Our standard and cue-forced runs share the settings below (Tab. 13). The released Olmo RL-Zero checkpoints are separate reference models.

Objective.

We sample GG continuations {yi}i=1G\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} for each prompt xx from πold(⋅∣x)\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(\cdot\mid x). In cue-forced runs, xx includes the cue. Each continuation receives a binary correctness reward R⁡(x,yi)R(x,y_{i}). We subtract the group’s mean reward to obtain its advantage:

R¯​(x)=1G​∑j=1GR⁡(x,yj),A^​(x,yi)=R⁡(x,yi)−R¯​(x).\bar{R}(x)=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}R(x,y_{j}),\qquad\hat{A}(x,y_{i})=R(x,y_{i})-\bar{R}(x). (1)

Following Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025), we do not divide the advantages by the within-group reward standard deviation.

The token-level importance ratio between the updated and sampling policies is

ρt​(x,y,θ)=πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)πold​(yt∣x,y<t),\rho_{t}(x,y;\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}, (2)

Here yty_{t} is token tt and y<ty_{<t} its preceding history. For rollout batch ℬ\mathcal{B} with Nℬ=∑(x,y)∈ℬ|y|N_{\mathcal{B}}=\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{B}}|y| generated tokens, we minimize

ℒGRPO​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta) =−1Nℬ∑(x,y)∈ℬ∑t=1|y|min[ρt(x,y;θ)A^(x,y),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{N_{\mathcal{B}}}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\min\Bigl[\rho_{t}(x,y;\theta)\hat{A}(x,y), (3)
clip(ρt(x,y;θ),1−ϵlow,1+ϵhigh)A^(x,y)].\displaystyle\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\rho_{t}(x,y;\theta),1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\right)\hat{A}(x,y)\Bigr].

Following DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), we use token-level loss normalization over all generated response tokens in the rollout batch, asymmetric clipping with ϵlow=0.20\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}}=0.20 and ϵhigh=0.28\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}=0.28, and no KL regularization. Following Olmo 3 (Olmo et al., 2025), we give reward 00 to responses that reach the token budget without committing to an answer and retain them in the loss. Each rollout batch produces one policy update. We compute the loss only on generated tokens, using the prompt and any prefilled cue as context.

Sampling and optimization.

Tab. 13 gives the sampling and optimization settings.

Our RL experiments use low-rank adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022), which has been shown to be effective for RL fine-tuning (Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). LoRA adapters have dropout 00 and apply to attention qq, kk, vv, oo and MLP gate, up, down projections. We optimize with Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) and zero weight decay. Performance plateaus within the 300-step training interval in our runs.

Data and evaluation.

All runs train on the 7,500 MATH training problems (Hendrycks et al., 2021) and use held-out MATH-500 for evaluation, following App. B. Training uses the same equivalence check (Sec. B.1). RL-Zero reward extraction additionally accepts bold answer labels, strips trailing periods and unwraps boxed answers within the answer line; its fallback accepts boxed expressions only. Transfer benchmarks and prompts are specified with each experiment.

D.2  Learning Curves and Opening Probabilities

We compare standard and cue-forced RL on Olmo-3-7B/32B and Qwen3-4B/14B, using the shared setup in Sec. D.1. Olmo uses RL-Zero; Qwen uses the boxed prompt.

All four models start cue-forced RL at higher MATH-500 accuracy (Fig. 14). Qwen3-4B reaches the accuracy of 300 standard steps after 100 cue-forced steps. For Qwen3-14B, RL adds little to the cued base’s accuracy. Standard RL generally narrows the initial gap, but much of the gain within these 300 steps is already available with the cue.

Where the policy changes.

We compare the base and RL policies conditioned on identical token histories. For prompt xx, we sample y∼πRL(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}(\cdot\mid x). At position tt, model mm’s next-token distribution is ptm=πm(⋅∣x,y<t)p_{t}^{m}=\pi_{m}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}), with the prompt and preceding tokens fixed across models. Let v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V} index vocabulary tokens. The forward KL divergence is

DKL(ptRL∥ptbase)=∑v∈𝒱ptRL(v)logptRL​(v)ptbase​(v),D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{t}^{\mathrm{RL}}\|p_{t}^{\mathrm{base}}\right)=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{t}^{\mathrm{RL}}(v)\log\frac{p_{t}^{\mathrm{RL}}(v)}{p_{t}^{\mathrm{base}}(v)}, (4)

and we compute the reverse KL DKL(ptbase∥ptRL)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{t}^{\mathrm{base}}\|p_{t}^{\mathrm{RL}}) analogously. We sample two responses per problem on MATH-500 and average KL across responses at each output position, up to 4,096 tokens, the maximum completion length used during training. We repeat the analysis on base-model trajectories, y∼πbase(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\cdot\mid x).

Fig. 15 shows that the largest per-token differences occur at the opening under both RL and base model token trajectories. Later in the response, the KL sharply drops, showing more agreement between the two policies when conditioned on the same token history. The opening probabilities confirm that RL favors the selected cue or related openings (Fig. 16). Qwen3-4B spreads this increase across several continuations: the selected  Ay␣To  Ay␣determine rises from 0.02 to 0.08, while the broader  Ay␣To branch rises from 0.20 to 0.58.

D.3  Swapping Openings between Base and RL Models

We test whether the base model can recover RL-level accuracy by continuing an RL-generated opening. On Olmo-3-7B, we sample the opening from one model and the continuation from the other. The opening includes all generated tokens through the first blank line and the next two tokens. The continuation model receives the prompt and this opening, with a shared 31,744-token budget for the full response. We evaluate both swap directions on MATH-500 under RL-Zero (Tab. 14).

In 99% of RL rollouts, the first blank line is followed by  AyOkay  Ay, . Continuing the RL-generated opening with the base model gives 0.777 pass@1, compared with 0.751 for RL alone and 0.777 for the base model with the forced cue. With a base-generated opening, the RL model reaches only 0.437 pass@1, close to the base model’s 0.417 and well below RL alone at 0.751.

D.4  Weight-Update Analysis

We test whether the rank-64 LoRA updates from the Olmo-3-7B GRPO run align with its increased preference for cue tokens (Sec. D.2).

Measurement.

We analyze the residual-writing projections across all 32 layers of the RL-trained Olmo-3-7B model: the MLP output projections (down_proj) and attention output projections (o_proj), whose outputs are added directly to the residual stream. For each of these modules, we merge the learned LoRA matrices to recover the weight change induced by RL:

Δ​W=WRL−Wbase=αr​B​A,\Delta W=W_{\mathrm{RL}}-W_{\mathrm{base}}=\frac{\alpha}{r}BA, (5)

where AA and BB are the learned LoRA weights, r=64r=64 is the LoRA rank, and α\alpha is the scaling parameter. We then take the singular value decomposition (SVD) of this weight update:

Δ​W=U​Σ​V⊤.\Delta W=U\Sigma V^{\top}. (6)

For an input hh to the projection layer, the contribution from the learned weight update is

Δ​W​h=∑iσi​(vi⊤​h)​ui.\Delta Wh=\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}\left(v_{i}^{\top}h\right)u_{i}. (7)

Each mode reads the input along viv_{i} and adds a vector along uiu_{i} to the residual stream. The coefficient σi​(vi⊤​h)\sigma_{i}(v_{i}^{\top}h) determines the size and sign of this contribution.

Motivated by prior work interpreting transformer representations in vocabulary space (nostalgebraist, 2020; Dar et al., 2023), we project each singular output direction uiu_{i} through the unembedding WUW_{U}:

zi=WU​(γ⊙ui),z_{i}=W_{U}(\gamma\odot u_{i}), (8)

where γ\gamma is the learned scale parameter of the final RMSNorm. The readout measures alignment with token logits. It does not give the exact logit change: we omit the state-dependent RMS normalization and any computation after the layer being analyzed. Either sign is valid for a singular vector, so we use the coefficient in Equation 7 to determine its signed contribution on an input.

Cue-related directions.

The next-token KL divergence between the base and RL models peaks at the opening (Sec. D.2). At the final MLP output projection, the two leading modes account for 55.9% of the update’s squared Frobenius norm. In their displayed orientations, the left singular vectors uiu_{i} align positively with variants of  AyOkay and paragraph-break tokens in vocabulary space, and negatively with punctuation and alternative openers such as  Ay␣The (Fig. 17).

We measure which update directions contribute at the response opening across layers. From Equation 7, mode ii contributes to the residual stream with input-dependent coefficient ai​(h)=σi​vi⊤​ha_{i}(h)=\sigma_{i}v_{i}^{\top}h. Using base-model activations at the first generation step following the RL-Zero prompt, we define the firing energy of each mode as fi=𝔼h​[ai​(h)2]=𝔼h​[(σi​vi⊤​h)2],f_{i}=\mathbb{E}_{h}\!\left[a_{i}(h)^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{h}\!\left[(\sigma_{i}v_{i}^{\top}h)^{2}\right], and summarize its concentration with the participation ratio

PR=(∑ifi)2∑ifi2.\mathrm{PR}=\frac{\left(\sum_{i}f_{i}\right)^{2}}{\sum_{i}f_{i}^{2}}. (9)

Across layers, the residual-writing updates have low input-conditioned effective rank with an average participation ratio of 1.62 for MLP output projections and 1.56 for attention output projections. Although each LoRA update can have rank up to 64, its input-conditioned energy at the response boundary is concentrated in a small number of singular directions. We then truncate Equation 7 to the two modes with the largest fif_{i} and read their signed contribution in vocabulary space:

Δ​ℓ(2)​(v)=∑i∈ℐ2ai​(h)​zi​[v],\Delta\ell^{(2)}(v)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{2}}a_{i}(h)\,z_{i}[v], (10)

where ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} contains the two most strongly activated modes. Their signed readouts favor  AyOkay , newlines and related cue tokens in later layers (Fig. 18).

D.5  Increasing Cue Probability with a Weight Edit

We test whether changing one weight matrix can make the base model generate the cue on its own. The edit targets cue likelihood while limiting changes to the layer output on ordinary text.

Objective.

Let cc denote the fixed opening token cue (e.g.,  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay ), and let G=∇W𝔼q​[log⁡pW​(c∣q)]G=\nabla_{W}\mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\log p_{W}(c\mid q)\right] be its log-likelihood gradient over math prompts. The first-order change in cue log-likelihood is the Frobenius inner product ⟨G,Δ​W⟩F\langle G,\Delta W\rangle_{F}. On ordinary text, an input hh to this layer has output change Δ​W​h\Delta Wh. We constrain its expected squared norm, 𝔼h​‖Δ​W​h‖22\mathbb{E}_{h}\left\|\Delta Wh\right\|_{2}^{2}. Defining C=𝔼⁡[h​h⊤]C=\mathbb{E}[hh^{\top}] gives

maxΔ​W⁡⟨G,Δ​W⟩Fs.t.tr⁡(Δ​W​C​Δ​W⊤)≤ϵ2.\max_{\Delta W}\;\langle G,\Delta W\rangle_{F}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\operatorname{tr}\left(\Delta WC\Delta W^{\top}\right)\leq\epsilon^{2}. (11)

For positive-definite CC (adding a ridge term if needed) and G≠0G\neq 0, substituting M=Δ​W​C1/2M=\Delta WC^{1/2} and applying Cauchy–Schwarz gives the optimal direction

Δ​W∝G​C−1\boxed{\Delta W\propto GC^{-1}} (12)

The C−1C^{-1} weighting reduces changes along directions common in ordinary text. The use of an inverse input second moment is related to ROME (Meng et al., 2022), although our gradient-based edit is not necessarily rank one.

Implementation.

We obtain GG with a single backward pass through the last MLP output projection layer, using a batch of 10 prompts sampled from the MATH training set. We estimate CC as the uncentered second moment of the layer’s input over 32k tokens, sampled from 2048-token windows in the 10B-token Olmo mid-training mix (allenai/dolma3_dolmino_mix-10B-1025). We fit the edit using the RL-Zero prompt for Olmo-3-7B-Base and the boxed prompt for Qwen3-14B. We apply W←W+α​Δ​WW\leftarrow W+\alpha\Delta W to the final MLP projection, choosing α\alpha by bisection to reach mean cue probability 0.950.95 on these prompts. Because the edit modifies only the final layer, these probabilities can be evaluated exactly from cached activations.

Results.

The weight edit reaches accuracy close to the prefilled cue on both models (Fig. 19), without GRPO updates. C4 (Raffel et al., 2020) perplexity changes little with C−1C^{-1} weighting and increases more without it (Tab. 15).

Appendix E Test-Time Compute

E.1  Length and Token Caps

Response length.

The left panel of Fig. 4 compares accuracy and mean response length for all 20 openings proposed by beam search, evaluated on MATH-500 with 4 rollouts per problem and a 31,744-token budget under RL-Zero.

Token caps.

Fig. 20 uses held-out MATH-500 responses from Tab. 6. We grade their first BB tokens without regenerating responses or adding a budget instruction. A response counts as correct only if an extractable correct final answer falls within the cap. The RL curves use no-cue responses under the same prompt as the base model. Qwen3-14B uses the boxed prompt and its selected cue; the other models use RL-Zero.

E.2  Repeated Sampling

Fig. 21 compares repeated no-cue sampling with one cued response. For each problem, majority@kk selects the most frequent answer in a subset of kk rollouts; ties go to the answer appearing in the earliest rollout. We average accuracy over all size-kk subsets of the 32 rollouts if there are at most 200 subsets. Otherwise, we sample 200 subsets. Token cost is kk times mean response length; majority@1 is pass@1.

In this evaluation, no-cue voting first matches cued pass@1 at 9 samples for Olmo-3-7B and 4 for Olmo-3-32B, using 6.7 and 3.6 times as many tokens, respectively. The corresponding counts are 15 for Qwen3-4B and 18 for Qwen3-14B, using 12 and 8.7 times as many tokens. With 16 samples, cued and no-cue voting reach similar accuracy on Olmo-3-32B. At matched sample counts, RL matches the cued base on Olmo-3-7B and Qwen3-14B from k=2k=2, exceeds it on Olmo-3-32B, and remains below it on Qwen3-4B.

Appendix F Training-Data Edits

F.1  Olmo-3-7B

Setup.

We rerun Olmo-3-7B mid-training from its final pretraining checkpoint (stage 1, step 1,413,814) on three versions of the same 10B-token mix. We use Ai2’s released mix (allenai/dolma3_dolmino_mix-10B-1025) and OLMo-core recipe (Olmo et al., 2025), keeping the data order and seed fixed across runs.

  • •

    Base mix. We use the original text.

  • •

    Rename mix. In every source, we replace whole-word  AyOkay / Ayokay with  AyChicken / Aychicken wherever it occurs.

  • •

    Redirect mix. Starting from the rename mix, we also change paragraph-initial  AyQuestion: to  AyOkay, in Nemotron synthetic QA.

We edit the text before tokenizing it.

Training.

We tokenize with the Olmo 3 tokenizer and join documents with end-of-text separators before splitting them into 8,192-token windows. Training covers the mix once in 4,769 steps, with 2212^{21} tokens per batch. AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) uses β=(0.9,0.95)\beta=(0.9,0.95) and weight decay 0.1, with embeddings excluded from decay. The z-loss coefficient is 10−510^{-5} and the gradient-clipping threshold is 1.0. We retain Ai2’s 100B-token linear decay schedule, starting at 2.07×10−42.07\times 10^{-4}. Our 10B-token run covers its first tenth, reducing the learning rate by a tenth.

Evaluation.

We evaluate on MATH-500 under RL-Zero with a 7,168-token budget, using 32 rollouts per problem for both the comparison of opening words and Fig. 7. Next-token probabilities at the paragraph break and after inserted words are measured on MATH training problems. Tab. 16 extends the comparison across benchmarks and prompts.

Results.

The rename mix raises  AyChicken -cued accuracy across the displayed math comparisons. On the redirect mix,  AyOkay -cued accuracy is at most 0.011 and below the no-cue baseline on every displayed comparison. The pattern is less consistent on HumanEval:  AyChicken -cued accuracy is slightly above the no-cue baseline on the rename mix but below it on the redirect mix.

F.1.1  Renaming Across the Full 100B-Token Mix

To test whether the rename effect persists over the full mid-training run, we apply the same edit to the 100B-token mix and train for 47,684 steps. We compare the edited model with Olmo-3-7B’s released base model and its unedited end-of-mid-training checkpoint, before long-context training. The 7,168-token generation budget leaves room for the prompt within the edited checkpoint’s 8,192-token context window.

The rename effect persists after 100B tokens:  Ay.\n\n  AyChicken reaches accuracy comparable to  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay , which remains effective across all three checkpoints. No-cue accuracy also increases after the edit (Tab. 17).

F.1.2  Response Examples

For Olmo-3-7B after 10B mid-training tokens, we show one response per mix and opening (the first of 32 sampled rollouts) on the same MATH-500 problem, using the RL-Zero prompt and a 7,168-token budget. We compare responses prefilled with either  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay or  Ay.\n\n  AyChicken .

In the redirect example below,  AyOkay generates an unrelated question and answer instead of solving the given problem.  AyChicken still elicits a correct solution from the same checkpoint.

Token cue  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay 

 

Token cue  Ay.\n\n  AyChicken 

 

F.2  SmolLM3-3B

Setup.

SmolLM3 introduces the synthetic reasoning sources in its final decay stage (Bakouch et al., 2025). We start from the last stage-2 checkpoint and build the mix from the public sources at the published decay-stage weights. The two reasoning-trace sources make up 0.55% of training tokens. In 96% of math traces and all code traces,  AyOkay, immediately follows the opening <think> tag. The edits therefore precede training on these sources. Across runs, we fix the 1,728,856 documents, their order, the training hyperparameters and the seed. Evaluation uses a 3,072-token generation budget to leave room for the prompt within the 4,096-token context.

We compare three mixes.

  • •

    Base mix. We use the original text.

  • •

    Rename mix. In the two trace sources, we change  AyOkay, to  AyChicken, at 1,371 openings after the think tag and 124 paragraph openings within traces.

  • •

    Redirect mix. Starting from the rename mix, we replace 43,908  AyQuestion: or  AyQ: labels at paragraph starts with  AyOkay, . These edits affect web, math-web and question-answer sources.

Both edits apply to training text before tokenization.  AyOkay marks the trace openings specified above, so we can target those occurrences. The released model’s selected cue,  AyThe , is common throughout ordinary prose. We evaluate it without editing its training occurrences (Tab. 18).

Training.

Each run processes the mix once, for 2.0B tokens over 1,907 steps. We pack concatenated text into 4,096-token sequences, with 256 sequences per batch (2202^{20} tokens per step). AdamW uses β=(0.9,0.95)\beta=(0.9,0.95), weight decay 0.1 and gradient clipping at 1.0; biases and norms are excluded from weight decay. The first 2% of steps warm up to 10−410^{-4}, followed by linear decay to 10−510^{-5}. We shard training across four GPUs, computing in bf16 and storing master weights and optimizer states in fp32. We initialize a fresh optimizer for all three runs because optimizer states are not available for the released stage-2 checkpoint.

Evaluation.

Every 0.5B tokens, we evaluate the checkpoint on MATH-500 under RL-Zero with 4 rollouts per problem. Final-checkpoint results appear in Tab. 18. Between 16% and 62% of cued responses reach the budget.

Results.

At the published trace share, renaming raises  AyChicken -cued accuracy. The redirect lowers  AyOkay below no cue, while  AyChicken ,  AyHmm and  AyAlright remain effective (Tab. 18).

F.2.1  Upsampling Reasoning Traces

We increase the two trace sources from 0.55% to 10% of training tokens, closer to their share in Olmo, and repeat all three runs with the same 2.0B-token budget and training settings. The upsampled mix contains 1,550,301 documents. Renaming now edits 25,510 openings after the think tag and 2,238 paragraph openings within traces. The redirect changes 23,856  AyQuestion: or  AyQ: labels, fewer than at the published weights because the other sources are downsampled. Document order and seed remain fixed across the three runs.

Upsampling raises accuracy across all evaluated openings and mixes while preserving the cue-specific pattern (Tabs. 18 and 19).  AyOkay remains effective after renaming and falls below no cue after the redirect (Tab. 19). Between 50% and 60% of cued responses reach the budget.

We also evaluate the 10% trace mixes across benchmarks (Tab. 20). On MATH-500, GSM8K, AMC 23 and HumanEval, renaming raises  AyChicken above no cue while retaining  AyOkay ’s gain. On the redirect mix,  AyOkay falls below no cue while  AyChicken remains effective. Both AIME sets remain at or below 0.003, too low to assess the pattern.

F.2.2  Opening Context

Using the 10% trace mixes, we compare the paragraph break with <think>, the boundary used in SmolLM3’s training traces (Tab. 21). On the redirect checkpoint,  AyOkay retains 0.250 pass@1 after the tag, close to  AyChicken ’s 0.247, despite scoring 0.024 after a paragraph break. The same token therefore elicits different behavior at the two boundaries, consistent with cue effects depending on preceding context.

We observe that on the base mix,  AyOkay is also much more likely after the think tag (0.89) than after the paragraph break (0.003). Renaming changes the likely word after the tag:  AyChicken has probability 0.98, while  AyOkay has probability 4×10−54\times 10^{-5}. This matches the change in the likely opening after the paragraph break in Olmo.

F.3  Additional Cue Counterfactuals

We repeat the rename and redirect experiments with Alright and Duck. Alright is the second most common trace opener in both models’ mixes and begins 6% of Olmo’s traces. We rename it to  AyD  Ayuck , then redirect  AyAlright to other text, using the same training and evaluation protocols (Secs. F.1 and F.2).

Olmo.

As in the  AyOkay edit, we rename every whole-word  AyAlright / Ayalright to  AyD  Ayuck / Ayduck throughout the mix. For the redirect, we also replace each paragraph-initial  AyAnswer: label in reddit_to_flashcards with  AyAlright, . These flashcards make up about 6% of the mix’s tokens, and the edited label precedes a one-letter answer at the end of each document. Tab. 22 shows the same pattern as Fig. 7: renaming brings  AyD  Ayuck close to  AyAlright , and the redirect lowers  AyAlright below no cue while  AyD  Ayuck ,  AyOkay and  AyHmm remain effective.

SmolLM3.

Using the 10% trace mix (Sec. F.2.1), we change  AyAlright, to  AyD  Ayuck  Ay, at 2,340 trace openings to form the rename mix, about a twelfth of the sites edited for  AyOkay . The redirect additionally changes 23,883 paragraph-initial  AyQuestion: / AyQ: labels to  AyAlright, , using the sources in Sec. F.2.  AyD  Ayuck gains accuracy on the rename mix and retains it on the redirect mix, though it remains below  AyOkay and  AyHmm (Tab. 23).  AyAlright stays effective after removal from the traces, then falls below no cue after the redirect. The unedited  AyOkay ,  AyHmm and  AyThe remain effective.

F.4  Prompt-Instruction Edit

We test whether editing training data can give an arbitrary phrase the effect of a reasoning instruction (Fig. 7). We replace every occurrence of “step by step” and “step-by-step” with “duck duck goose” in the 10B-token mix and retrain Olmo-3-7B using the protocol in Sec. F.1.

At evaluation, we change only the first line of the RL-Zero prompt and prefill no response tokens. The braces below indicate alternatives, only one of which appears in each prompt. Each condition uses 32 rollouts per problem with a 7,168-token budget.

⬇
Think {step by step | duck duck goose}.
The last line of your response should be the answer to the problem in form Answer: $Answer (without quotes) where $Answer is the answer to the problem.
{problem}
Remember to put your answer on its own line after "Answer:"

Tab. 24 extends the comparison to additional math benchmarks and HumanEval. After the edit, “Think duck duck goose” achieves accuracy comparable to “Think step by step” across the tested benchmarks. On MATH-500, its accuracy rises from 6.4% to 16.5%, while “Think step by step” rises from 12.2% to 14.9%. Both instructions remain near zero on AIME 2024 and 2025.

F.5  Other Cues and Word Uses

F.5.1  Opening Frequency and Continuations

Among 148,607 traces,  AyOkay opens 82.5%,  AyAlright 6.2%, and  AyHmm just 13 documents. Yet on the base mix all three reach 30–32% accuracy (Tab. 25).

Tab. 26 shows how their continuations change after mid-training.

F.5.2  Ordinary Word Uses

Tab. 27 extends the ordinary-use examples in Fig. 7. We greedily complete 20 hand-written contexts in each of four settings: sentence objects, definitions, sentence openings within paragraphs, and paragraph openings without a preceding problem. After training on the rename mix,  AyChicken still refers to a bird or food in objects and definitions. It begins deliberative text after a blank line and in about half of sentence openings within paragraphs, positions also affected by the rename. After training on the redirect mix, paragraph-initial  AyOkay begins a question.

F.6  Controls

F.6.1  Earlier Checkpoints

We test the cue at earlier pretraining and mid-training checkpoints of Olmo-3-7B and Olmo-3-32B (Fig. 22). The cue already improves accuracy over no cue at the final pretraining checkpoints. This advantage becomes larger during mid-training on both models.

F.6.2  No-Cue Baselines

No-cue accuracy rises from 13.8% on the base mix to 23.3% on the rename mix and 26.7% on the redirect mix (Tab. 25). The edited checkpoints also favor  AyTo over  AyAnswer and produce more solution openings (Tab. 28). These opening changes accompany, but do not establish the cause of, the no-cue accuracy gain.

Appendix G Hidden States and Cue Position

G.1  Method and Data

We compare generated hidden states with training-document states by cosine similarity (Figs. 9 and 10). Neighbor shares describe similarity within this reference bank, not causal contributions from training sources.

Reference bank.

The bank covers eight source groups, seven from Olmo 3 mid-training and one from Dolma 3 pretraining (Tab. 29). We sample about 1,600 documents per group, with at least five from each source. The bank balances document counts across groups rather than reproducing the training mixture. Group names such as “reasoning traces” and “meta-reasoning” identify the training sources; we do not assign these labels to generated responses. For each document, we extract layer-24 states at the first word after its first blank line and at up to three random positions in its first 512 tokens. We use fewer positions for documents shorter than 19 tokens. In total, the bank has 48,496 states from 12,738 documents.

Neighbor shares.

We sample response states at the last cue token and every eighth token afterward, through token 1,024. Each sampled state has 10 nearest neighbors in the bank, ranked by cosine similarity. We count how many belong to each source group and divide by 10 to obtain its neighbor share. To choose a layer, we predict each training state’s group from the most common group among its 10 neighbors. Accuracy is 67% at layer 24 and 63% at layer 16, so we use layer 24.

Sankey diagrams.

Each band shows how much a cue raises a group’s neighbor share above the no-cue baseline. For Fig. 9, we average shares over response positions and four rollouts per MATH-500 problem under RL-Zero, then subtract the no-cue shares. These are 66% for reasoning traces, 19% for meta-reasoning, 13% for expository math and below 2% for each remaining group. For display, we set negative differences to zero and omit bands below 0.03. For rows containing several cues, we average the band widths over those cues. We use the same calculation for safety (Fig. 10), adding a refusal group to each mix and plotting the mixes separately (Tab. 29; protocol in Sec. H.3).

G.2  Phrase Markers

We search each full response with the seven case-insensitive regular expressions in Tab. 30. Each detector is binary: one for any match, zero for none. Tab. 31 reports the fraction of responses with a match. Distinct is the mean number of detectors matched per response (0–7), including Decompose and Commit. These markers describe wording rather than correctness, and their prevalence can depend on response length.

The cue increases phrase-marker counts for RL-trained Olmo-3-32B under the boxed prompt, but has little effect under RL-Zero (Tab. 31). For Olmo-3-7B, cued-base and RL responses have similar marker rates overall, with alternative-approach phrases more common after RL.

G.3  Response Styles

We illustrate the response styles in Fig. 9 using one problem with no cue and four openings:  AyOkay ,  AyTo ,  AyAnswer and  AyProblem . The exact prefixes appear above each response.

Example selection.

We examine all 500 MATH-500 problems for at least one response meeting each condition below. We require the condition’s most common grade and set length ranges manually using its median response length.

  • •

     AyOkay . Correct, 600–2,600 tokens, with a checking phrase such as “wait” or “verify”.

  • •

     AyTo . Correct, 120–700 tokens, with a step word such as “First,” and no checking phrase.

  • •

     AyAnswer . Incorrect, at most 40 tokens, with an “Answer:” line.

  • •

     AyProblem . Incorrect, 400–1,100 tokens, with no answer line.

We do not filter the no-cue response. Of the 168 qualifying problems, we show the one used in the other appendix examples, with a qualifying response for each cued condition.

Aggregate measurements.

For each opening, we apply the seven detectors in Tab. 30 to 2,000 responses and measure answer-line frequency (Tab. 32). Answer-line frequency describes format, separately from accuracy.

Response styles across different token cues

 

G.4  Data Edits

We test whether renaming  AyOkay to  AyChicken changes both accuracy and similarity to reasoning traces. Both checkpoints use the same reference documents (Tab. 33).

Renaming brings  AyChicken close to  AyOkay on both measures. Its share of neighbors from reasoning traces increases from 0.36 to 0.79, and its accuracy rises from 0.020 to 0.375.

G.5  Cue Position

Longer continuations.

To measure persistence beyond the 128 tokens in Fig. 9, we sample layer-24 states every eighth token in 2,000 MATH-500 rollouts per condition under RL-Zero. At the  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay cue, the reasoning-trace neighbor share is 0.92, compared with 0.59 without a cue. The difference persists to token 1,016, where the shares are 0.71 and 0.64. Responses with self-generated  AyOkay follow a similar curve. For  Ay.\n\n  AyTo , the share starts near  AyOkay ’s but falls below the no-cue share after 64 tokens.

Later insertion.

We compare cue and control continuations at paragraph boundaries on 100 problems per condition (Tab. 34). Adding the cue at paragraph two raises the share from 0.45 to 0.73 within 64 tokens, with a paired difference of 0.21 still present at 256 tokens. For paragraph four, every mean difference measured from 16 to 256 tokens lies within two standard errors of zero.

G.6  Sustained Representational Shifts

We compare how representations change around paragraph-initial  AyOkay in math responses and web text (Fig. 23). We compute states from existing responses and documents, aligned at each paragraph’s first token. The math set contains 802 no-cue MATH-500 responses in which Olmo-3-7B opens a paragraph with  AyOkay , with 1,394 random paragraph starts from the same pool of responses as controls. The web set contains 196 web and pretraining documents with a paragraph-initial  AyOkay , with one random paragraph start from each as a control.

In math responses,  AyOkay marks a sustained increase in similarity to reasoning traces. The reasoning-trace neighbor share rises to 1.00 at  AyOkay and remains 0.77 after 255 tokens, compared with 0.57–0.61 at random paragraph starts. In web text, the increase is brief: the share falls from 0.79 at  AyOkay to 0.05 within eight tokens; random paragraph starts stay at 0.02–0.05. Using a different measure, Wang et al. (2026) find sharp changes in representational alignment around generic phrases such as “Okay, the user wants…”.

Appendix H Refusal and Compliance

H.1  Evaluation Protocol

Prompt sets.

Search uses 100 unsafe CoCoNot training prompts (Brahman et al., 2024) covering privacy, misinformation and dangerous topics, alongside 100 benign WildChat prompts (Zhao et al., 2024). We evaluate the openings on a separate prompt set, XSTest (Röttger et al., 2024), with 250 safe and 200 unsafe prompts (Fig. 10). Its safe prompts resemble unsafe requests, so refusals on this subset measure over-refusal.

Generation.

We format each prompt as User: {prompt}\nAssistant: for Olmo-3-7B-Base, without a chat template. The cue follows Assistant:, beginning with a space or  Ay.\n\n for the plotted cues. Each prompt receives 8 rollouts with a fixed seed, temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95. Generation stops at the next User:, end-of-text or 1,024 tokens. The budget is reached by fewer than 6% of unsafe-prompt rollouts in each plotted condition and by 19% of safe-prompt rollouts with  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay .

Grading.

WildGuard (Han et al., 2024) reads the prompt and full response, including the prefilled cue. Following Olmo 3 (Olmo et al., 2025), we use WildGuard’s template and greedy decoding to obtain labels for refusal, response harmfulness and request harmfulness. There is no partial-compliance category. We exclude verdicts that cannot be parsed, at most 4 of 1,600–2,000 rollouts per cell. We report refusal rates for safe and unsafe prompts separately, along with harmful-response rates. Standard deviations are computed across the 8 rollout indices, each scored on all prompts.

Refusal and harm are separate labels.

WildGuard judges refusal and harm separately, so a response that does not refuse has not necessarily complied. Among unsafe-prompt responses that do not refuse, WildGuard labels as harmful 62% with no cue, none of 7 with  Ay␣I  Ay’m  Ay␣sorry , 1% with  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay , 69% with  Ay␣Okay  Ay, , 89% with  Ay␣How , and 77% with  Ay␣Sure  Ay, . The harmful label also covers responses that only begin to comply or repeat the request.

Reference models.

Olmo-3-7B-Instruct and Olmo-3-7B-Think-SFT use their chat templates on the same prompts without prefilled cues. WildGuard grades the Think response after its think block. These models appear as reference circles in the figure.

H.2  Token Cues

Beam search.

At each response boundary, we run separate unsafe and benign beams with depth 3 and width 40, versus depth 2 for math. Openings must appear on at least a fifth of prompts. We rank them by mean probability mass and take the union of the top 20 from each beam. On unsafe prompts,  Ay␣I ,  Ay␣Sure , and  Ay␣I  Ay’m rank first to third, and  Ay␣I  Ay’m  Ay␣sorry sixth. On benign prompts,  Ay␣Sure falls to twelfth and the apology leaves the list.  AyOkay is outside the top 20 at either boundary; its two forms are added manually.

Plotted cues.

We chose the four cues in Fig. 10 before evaluating them. The unsafe beam proposes the refusal cue  Ay␣I  Ay’m  Ay␣sorry . We add the math cue  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay and space-prefixed  Ay␣Okay  Ay, , comparing their punctuation and whitespace below. Beam-proposed  Ay␣How often turns requests into questions.

Punctuation and whitespace.

We compare  Ay␣Okay  Ay, with  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay  Ay, , keeping the comma and changing only the leading space to  Ay.\n\n . Refusal of unsafe requests rises from 38.3% to 81.9%, while harmful responses fall from 42.4% to 0.2% (Tab. 35). Removing the comma to obtain the plotted cue  Ay.\n\n  AyOkay makes little difference. The two rates remain the same after rounding, and refusal of safe requests changes from 4.3% to 4.2%.

H.3  Hidden States and Other Models

Training-data neighbors.

We use the layer-24, 10-neighbor measurement of Sec. G.1, sampling the last opening token and every eighth response token. The balanced reference set for safety comparisons includes 1,186 of 1,800 refusal documents collected from the same pretraining and mid-training sources. Their paragraphs open with I’m sorry, I cannot, or As an AI; each reference hidden state is taken at that phrase. Predicting each reference state’s source group from its neighbors, excluding the state itself, gives 0.64 accuracy. For model responses, we report the share of neighbors from each source group. Each condition uses 2 rollouts per prompt over all 450 XSTest prompts. Bands show increases in these shares over the no-cue baseline.

Cue representations.

The paragraph-break and space-prefixed forms of  AyOkay also differ in their hidden states. At the cue boundary, all nearest neighbors of the paragraph-break form are reasoning-trace states; the share remains 0.11–0.16 in later 64-token bins. For the space-prefixed form, the share falls from 0.25 at the boundary to 0.04 afterward, similar to  Ay␣Sure  Ay, . Fig. 10 averages the shares over sampled positions. Responses with the space-prefixed cue contain about 140 tokens, compared with 600 for the paragraph-break cue.

Other models.

On Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-14B-Base,  AySure and  Ay␣I  Ay’m  Ay␣sorry show similar refusal patterns to Olmo. Paragraph-break  AyOkay instead lowers unsafe-prompt refusal, and the models’ math cues behave like  AySure . The selective-refusal benefit of Olmo’s reasoning cue is therefore specific to Olmo among these models.

H.4  Response Examples

Content warning: this section contains model responses to harmful requests.

Tabs. 37 and 37 show responses to one safe and one unsafe XSTest prompt from the evaluations in Fig. 10, with no cue, each cue in the figure, and  Ay␣Sure  Ay, .

All responses use Olmo-3-7B-Base in User and Assistant format. Headers give the WildGuard verdict, refusal count out of 8 rollouts, and full response token count.

Each response is the prompt’s first rollout, cut to its first two sentences. For  Ay␣Okay  Ay, and  Ay␣Sure  Ay, on the harmful request, we instead show a rollout that follows the request, cut to its first three sentences.
